docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
I am an aspiring Geospatial Professional pursuing an MSc in Applied Geoinformatics at Paris Lodron Universität Salzburg. With expertise in GIS, remote sensing, spatial analysis, and geospatial programming, I work at the intersection of geography and data to transform complex spatial information into meaningful insights. My experience includes satellite and drone data processing, cartographic visualization, spatial database management, and geospatial analytics. As I continue to expand my capabilities in GeoAI, deep learning, and advanced remote sensing, I remain committed to leveraging geospatial technology to address real-world challenges and support informed decision-making.

docs.title: GIS Intern — Department of Irrigation, Assam
docs.text:
July 2024 – August 2024 | Guwahati, India

  • Delineated the catchment area of the Batha River Ubhati Outlet using QGIS 3.16.0 to support irrigation planning and water resource management.
  • Analyzed topographic and hydrological data to identify watershed boundaries and map the catchment.
  • Worked with engineers to apply the results to irrigation planning.
  • Prepared technical reports documenting the delineation for departmental use.

docs.title: GIS Trainee (Virtual Summer Intern) — GeoVigyan
docs.text:
June 2024 – July 2024 | Guwahati, India

  • Assessed forest health and land use/land cover (LULC) change in Palamau Tiger Reserve, Jharkhand, using Google Earth Engine and ArcGIS 10.7.1 with Landsat 8 imagery from USGS Earth Explorer.
  • Mapped and quantified LULC changes (vegetation, agriculture, built-up, water) using Random Forest classification with accuracy assessment.
  • Evaluated forest health with an NDVI-based Forest Health Index, identifying predominantly "average" vegetation condition shaped by seasonal, human, and natural stressors.
  • Produced geospatial insights to support environmental monitoring, conservation planning, and sustainable management.

A selection of my geospatial projects. Click any card to see the full write-up.

Cloud-Native Sentinel-2 Workflow: Guwahati

A cloud-native Earth observation pipeline for Guwahati, Assam. Sentinel-2 scenes were found through a STAC API, loaded lazily into an Xarray data cube, stored as Zarr, and used to derive a false-colour composite and NDVI vegetation map.

STAC Xarray Zarr Sentinel-2 NDVI Python

View Project →

World Population Mapping

Mapped 2024 country-level population and population density worldwide by joining World Bank population data to world country boundaries. The density map on a logarithmic scale shows that Malta and Bangladesh are the most densely populated countries.

jupyter geopandas pandas matplotlib request

View Project →

Flood Susceptibility Mapping of Kaziranga National Park

A GIS-based Weighted Overlay Analysis of flood susceptibility in Kaziranga National Park, Assam. Six terrain, hydrological, climatic and land cover layers from 2017 were combined into a single index and classified into four susceptibility zones.

docs.title: Cloud-Native Sentinel-2 Workflow: Guwahati, Assam¶
docs.text:
STAC · Planetary Computer · odc-stac · Xarray · Zarr · NDVI

This notebook shows an end-to-end, cloud-native Earth observation workflow over Guwahati, Assam (India). Instead of downloading whole satellite scenes, it queries a STAC catalogue, builds a lazy data cube from Cloud Optimised GeoTIFFs (COGs), and only pulls the pixels it needs into a local, chunked Zarr store for fast re-use.

Step What happens Pixels downloaded 1 Connect to the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API 0 2 Search Sentinel-2 L2A scenes (AOI, dates, cloud cover) 0 3 Build a lazy 3D Xarray dataset with odc-stac 0 4 Persist the cube to a local Zarr store Yes (once) 5 Re-open from Zarr and derive a False-Colour Composite and NDVI No (local)

Data: Sentinel-2 Level-2A (sentinel-2-l2a), bands B08 (NIR), B04 (Red), B03 (Green) Area of interest: 91.669, 26.097, 91.872, 26.218 (lon/lat bounding box, EPSG:4326) Period: 1 Oct – 30 Nov 2026, scenes with < 15 % cloud cover

docs.title: 1. Connect to the STAC API¶
docs.text: The Planetary Computer hosts assets in Azure Blob Storage behind short-lived SAS tokens. Passing sign_inplace as a modifier signs every asset URL automatically.

docs.title: 2. Search for scenes¶
docs.text: Only metadata is queried here. Filters: collection, bounding box (drawn with bboxfinder.com), date range (YYYY-MM-DD/YYYY-MM-DD) and a cloud-cover threshold.

docs.title: 3. Build a lazy data cube¶
docs.text:
odc.stac.load converts the STAC item collection into an xarray.Dataset with dimensions (time, y, x). Nothing is downloaded at this stage; Dask only stores the recipe for reading each chunk.

  • resolution=200 downsamples to 200 m for a fast, lightweight demo. Use 10 for full Sentinel-2 resolution.
  • groupby="solarday" merges tiles captured on the same solar day into one time step.
  • crs="EPSG:32646" reprojects to UTM zone 46N, which suits Assam.

docs.title: Quick look: False-Colour Composite (NIR-Red-Green)¶
docs.text: Mapping NIR to the red channel makes healthy vegetation appear bright red, water dark and built-up areas grey-cyan. Computing this plot triggers the first real data read.

docs.title: 4. Persist to Zarr¶
docs.text: Writing to Zarr downloads the pixels once and stores them as compressed, chunked arrays on local disk. Later analysis then reads from disk instead of the network.

docs.title: 5. Re-open the local store¶
docs.text: The Zarr store opens almost instantly because only metadata is read; chunks are loaded on demand.

docs.title: 7. NDVI¶
docs.text:
\[NDVI = \frac{NIR - Red}{NIR + Red}\]

Sentinel-2 L2A scenes processed with baseline ≥ 04.00 (since January 2022) carry a +1000 DN radiometric offset. The helper below masks no-data (0) and converts digital numbers to surface reflectance before computing the index. If your cube is already float reflectance, the step is skipped.

docs.title: Temporal median NDVI¶
docs.text: Taking the median across all clear scenes suppresses residual cloud, shadow and haze, giving a more stable picture of vegetation across the Oct–Nov window.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• A STAC search over Sentinel-2 L2A returned 13 low-cloud scenes for Guwahati with no pixels downloaded.
  • odc-stac assembled them into a lazy, Dask-backed (time, y, x) cube.
  • The cube was written once to Zarr and re-opened locally for fast analysis.
  • A false-colour composite and NDVI (single date and temporal median) were produced from the local store.

Possible extensions: run at 10 m resolution, add the SCL band for cloud masking, build an NDVI time series, or compare against the monsoon season.

Data: Copernicus Sentinel-2 (ESA), accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
I processed overlapping drone images of three very different landscapes in Pix4D, an urban neighbourhood in Assam, an open-pit mine in Switzerland and a village in Karnataka. For each area I generated a Point Cloud, Orthomosaic, Digital Surface Model (DSM), Digital Terrain Model (DTM) and Contours. The orthomosaics were then draped over the terrain in ArcScene for 3D visualisation.

Study Areas: Urban area (Panjabari, Assam), mining area (Switzerland), village area (Karnataka) Completed: August 2026 Context: PG Diploma in Geoinformatics, Accelcraft Institute of Geoinformatics Technology Role: Solo project Status: Completed

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Data Sources

  • Overlapping drone (UAV) image sets for three areas of interest (AOIs)
  • Esri satellite imagery as the QGIS basemap for checking the outputs

Processing Steps

  1. Imported the drone images for each AOI into a new Pix4D project.
  2. Aligned and calibrated the images using Structure from Motion (SfM), which reconstructs the terrain from overlapping photographs.
  3. Generated a dense Point Cloud for each area.
  4. Produced the DSM (surface including trees and buildings), the DTM (bare earth) and the Orthomosaic.
  5. Derived Contours from the DTM.
  6. Overlaid the orthomosaic and contours on the Esri satellite basemap in QGIS to check alignment.
  7. Draped each orthomosaic over its terrain in ArcScene for 3D visualisation.

Tools Used

Tool Purpose Pix4D Image alignment, Point Cloud, Orthomosaic, DSM, DTM and Contours QGIS Overlaying orthomosaics and contours on the Esri satellite basemap ArcScene 3D visualisation of the orthomosaics Agisoft Metashape Studied as an alternative photogrammetry workflow (alignment, dense cloud, mesh, texture)

docs.text: Output What it shows Typical uses Point Cloud Millions of 3D (X, Y, Z) points describing terrain, vegetation and buildings Terrain analysis, 3D visualisation, volume calculation Orthomosaic Geometrically corrected, stitched aerial map Land cover mapping, urban planning, infrastructure monitoring DSM Elevation of the surface including trees and buildings Building heights, flood modelling, line-of-sight analysis DTM Bare-earth elevation Watershed analysis, slope, hydrological modelling Contours Lines of equal elevation derived from the DTM Topographic mapping, route planning, engineering surveys

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
• Pix4D produced a full set of outputs (Point Cloud, Orthomosaic, DSM, DTM and Contours) for all three areas, even though they differ in terrain and land use.
  • The mining area shows the clearest relief. Tightly spaced contours follow the stepped benches of the pit, and the 3D view makes the benches easy to see.
  • The urban and village areas are gentler, so their contours are sparse. Their orthomosaics are most useful for mapping buildings, roads and land use.
  • Draping the orthomosaics in ArcScene turns flat maps into models that are easier to interpret and present.
  • The same outputs support surveying, mining volume estimates, hydrology and urban planning.
  • Limitations: positional accuracy depends on georeferencing, and adding Ground Control Points (GCPs) would improve it. Future work could compare Pix4D against Agisoft Metashape on the same image sets and calculate stockpile or pit volumes for the mine.

docs.title: Flood Susceptibility Mapping of Kaziranga National Park Using Weighted Overlay Analysis
Overview
docs.text:
I mapped flood susceptibility in Kaziranga National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site on the Brahmaputra floodplain, using a GIS-based multi-criteria Weighted Overlay Analysis. I combined six terrain, hydrological, climatic and land cover layers from 2017 into a single susceptibility index. The map can help with flood preparedness and wildlife protection planning in the park.

Study Area: Kaziranga National Park, Assam, India (~431.83 km²) Duration: March 2026 – March 2026 (16 March – 30 March) Role: Solo project Status: Completed

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Data Sources

  • Park boundary: World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) via Protected Planet
  • Elevation: SRTM DEM (30 m) via Google Earth Engine
  • Land cover: Landsat 8 Level-2, Collection 2, Tier 1 surface reflectance (2017) via Google Earth Engine
  • Rainfall: CHIRPS daily precipitation, aggregated to 2017 annual totals in Google Earth Engine
  • River network: HydroRIVERS (HydroSHEDS)

Processing Steps

  1. Filled voids and sinks in the DEM, then derived slope and flow accumulation.
  2. Clipped all layers to the park boundary, projected them to WGS 84 / UTM Zone 46N, and resampled them to a common 30 m grid.
  3. Classified Landsat 8 imagery into five land cover classes: water body, dense forest, agriculture, sandbar and grassland.
  4. Reclassified every layer to a 1–5 susceptibility scale. Low elevation, gentle slope and short distance to rivers score high. High flow accumulation and high rainfall also score high.
  5. Assigned influence weights (summing to 100%) and ran the Weighted Overlay in ArcMap using FSI = Σ(Wᵢ × Xᵢ).
  6. Classified the output into Low, Moderate, High and Very High zones and calculated the area of each.

Layer Weights

Layer Influence Euclidean Distance from River 25% Flow Accumulation 20% Annual Rainfall 20% Land Use / Land Cover 15% Digital Elevation Model 10% Slope 10%

Tools Used

Tool Purpose ArcMap 10.8 (Spatial Analyst) Terrain derivatives, Euclidean distance, reclassification and Weighted Overlay Google Earth Engine Accessing SRTM and Landsat 8, and aggregating CHIRPS rainfall HydroSHEDS / HydroRIVERS River network for distance and stream analysis

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
• 70.73% of the park (305.41 km²) falls in the Moderate susceptibility class.
  • 24.19% (104.45 km²) falls in the High class, concentrated in low-lying areas and along river channels.
  • Low susceptibility covers 21.94 km² (5.08%), and Very High only 0.03 km² (0.01%).
  • Elevation across the study extent ranges from 52 m to 785 m, and 2017 annual rainfall from about 2,110 to 2,760 mm.
  • Terrain is mostly low and gentle-sloped, and the river network is dense. This explains why most of the park falls in the Moderate to High classes.
  • Limitations: the model used a 30 m DEM and single-year rainfall, and it has no quantitative validation against historical flood extents. Future work could add Sentinel-1 SAR validation, AHP-based weights and machine learning models.

docs.title: Overview¶
docs.text:
Mapped 2024 country-level population and population density worldwide by joining World Bank population statistics to a world country boundary dataset. Choropleth maps show where people live, from raw population counts to density on a logarithmic scale.

Study Area: Global (all countries) Duration: [Start month/year – End month/year] Role: [Solo project / Team lead / Contributor] Status: [Completed / In progress]

docs.title: Methods & Tools¶
docs.text:
Data Sources

  • World country boundaries (GeoJSON): johan/world.geo.json
  • Population, total (SP.POP.TOTL): World Bank API

Processing Steps

  1. Load and inspect world country boundaries
  2. Load population data from the World Bank API and check for missing values
  3. Filter to 2024 and join population to boundaries on ISO3 country codes
  4. Map total population by country
  5. Reproject to an equal-area CRS, compute population density, and map it on a log scale

Tools Used

Tool Purpose geopandas Reading boundaries, spatial joins, reprojection, area calculation pandas Data loading, cleaning, aggregation requests Fetching data from the World Bank API matplotlib Static maps

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: World country boundaries and World Bank population records (1960–2025).

docs.title: Key Findings¶
docs.text:
• Population records were matched for 171 of the 266 World Bank entities in 2024; the remainder are regional aggregates (e.g. Arab World) with no matching country boundary
  • 9 boundary polygons have no 2024 population value (e.g. Antarctica, Taiwan & Kosovo(mismatch id/code), Western Sahara) and are shown in grey
  • Malta (~2,077 people/km²) and Bangladesh (~1,298 people/km²) have the highest population density among mapped countries
  • A logarithmic colour scale is needed for density, since values span several orders of magnitude
